title: Effectiveness of Monetary Policy Transmission in Morocco amid Reforms to the Monetary Policy Framework
abstract: This paper assesses the effectiveness of Morocco’s monetary policy transmission since 2018 in light of reforms aimed at modernizing the policy framework. Over the past decade, Morocco has introduced greater exchange rate flexibility, strengthened the legal and operational focus on price stability, and enhanced central bank communication—measures intended to anchor inflation expectations and improve transmission. Drawing on several years of post-reform data, we use a two-step empirical strategy: (i) identifying exogenous monetary policy shocks through a Taylor-rule-based approach leveraging Bank Al-Maghrib’s forecasts, and (ii) estimating their dynamic effects via local projections, a flexible approach well suited to settings with structural change and limited data. Our findings indicate that transmission to output and inflation has strengthened post-reform: a 1 percentage point policy rate hike reduces output by about 0.3 percent and inflation by 0.1 percent, compared to 0.1 and 0.05 percent pre-reform, respectively. However, responses remain delayed and muted relative to benchmark estimates for other emerging markets. Analysis of transmission channels shows the interest rate channel is most active, the credit channel is partially effective, and the exchange rate channel is stronger post-reform, while the asset price and expectations channels remain weak. These findings provide important insights for Morocco’s ongoing transition to an inflation targeting regime.

title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal
abstract: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
title: Cash Transfers in Developing Countries: Local Multipliers, Aggregate Effects, and External Adjustment
abstract: This paper studies the local and aggregate effects of cash transfers in developing countries, and how both change as the cash transfer program scales up. We build a two-region New Keynesian small open economy model and calibrate it to rich pre-treatment microdata from an ongoing cash transfer experiment in Malawi. The model implies a local multiplier on temporary transfers of about one, which depends on price stickiness, the share of liquidity-constrained households, and home bias in consumption. Spillovers to the rest of the country are negative under Malawi’s restricted international capital mobility and parallel exchange rate regimes, as cash transfers appreciate the real exchange rate and reduce exports. Consequently, the aggregate multiplier is less than the local multiplier. As the program scales up, the local multiplier converges toward the aggregate multiplier, so a scaled-up program may have smaller multipliers than micro-level estimates suggest. However, with unrestricted capital mobility, spillovers can be positive, especially under a fixed exchange rate. These results highlight the importance of the macroeconomic policy environment for aggregate multipliers and the effects of scaled-up transfer programs.

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

title: Hours or Heads? Demand Shocks and Labour Market Adjustments in Poland
abstract: This paper investigates the role of demand shocks in driving labour market dynamics in Poland, an economy that transitioned from very high to low and stable unemployment despite repeated adverse shocks. Our contribution is threefold. First, we propose two complementary sign-restricted Bayesian VAR models that distinguish between labour-extensive and labour-intensive aggregate demand shocks, where the former operate primarily through changes in employment, while the latter mainly affect workers’ effort and hours per worker. Despite different specifications, both models yield highly consistent results. Second, we find that labour-extensive demand shocks are a key driver of unemployment, labour-intensive demand shocks primarily affect output, prices, and productivity, whereas both shocks are similarly important for hours per worker. Third, we document that the relative importance of these shocks changes over time, suggesting that the dominant margin of labour market adjustment may depend on economic conditions and the policy environment.

title: Nowcasting Economic Activity in Afghanistan
abstract: Sound economic policy formulation requires high frequency economic activity data. This is particularly challenging in low-income, fragile, and conflict-affected states, such as Afghanistan, where quarterly GDP data is unavailable and annual GDP figures are published with considerable delays. This paper utilizes an innovative approach for estimating quarterly economic activity under these constraints, facilitating timely economic assessments in Afghanistan. Quarterly GDP data are interpolated from annual figures, utilizing money supply as a proxy indicator of economic activities due to Afghanistan’s predominately cash-based economy. By leveraging machine learning, traditional (macroeconomic), non-traditional (satellite) data, the approach provides real-time insights of the underlying direction of the Afghan economy at relatively high frequency and with partial information.

title: Manipulation-Robust Prediction
abstract: An increasing number of decisions are guided by machine learning algorithms. But when consequential decisions are encoded in algorithms, individuals may strategically alter their behavior to achieve desired outcomes. This paper develops an empirical approach that adjusts decision algorithms to anticipate manipulation. By explicitly modeling incentives to manipulate, our approach produces decision rules that are stable under manipulation, even when the rules are fully transparent. We stress-test this approach through a large field experiment in Kenya. When implemented, linear strategy-robust decision rules outperform standard linear models such as LASSO. (JEL C45, C93, D12, D91, G51, O12, O16)

source: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks,
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the extent to which an immigration shock to a region propagates through supply chains. Using the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees, who are densely concentrated in border regions of Turkey, we estimate how firms across the country are affected in terms of sales, employment, and wages. We also examine the impact of the shock on interprovincial trade, focusing on trade volume and network formation. The results reveal positive spillover effects of immigration for firms with pre-existing links to Syrian refugee-hosting regions through upstream and downstream supply chain connections. Furthermore, we find evidence that the shock expands inter-provincial trade and contributes to the formation of new firm-to-firm linkages between provinces. Finally, we show that traditional spatial approaches that compare regions with differing migration rates may conflate cross-province propagation with the direct effect of migrants; in our setting, this conflation overstates direct effects on sales and employment at both the firm and regional levels of aggregation and masks a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.

title: Household demand for retail bonds and time deposits: The case of Poland - replication package
abstract: This is the replication package for the paper Łesyk, M., Wesołowski, G., 2026. Household demand for retail bonds and time deposits: The case of Poland. This repository contains the data and R code which replicates all empirical results, figures, and tables included in the above-mentioned article. Abstract: We examine household demand for retail government bonds and time deposits in Poland, a small open economy where households can purchase government bonds directly. Our analysis extends a literature focused on the U.S., where indirect household Treasury debt holdings dominate. Using issue-level data, we construct a bond aggregate and estimate the elasticity of substitution between bonds and deposits. We find that these assets are imperfect substitutes, with an estimated elasticity somewhat above the U.S. benchmark. Interestingly, when longer-maturity bonds are excluded from the bond aggregate we cannot reject perfect substitution with time deposits. Next, we construct a broader asset aggregate of bonds and deposits and find that demand for it is negatively related to the opportunity-cost spread, consistent with theory and U.S. evidence. Our findings suggest effective monetary policy transmission to household assets and a need for active bond issuance policy in countries like Poland. Availability Status of the Data: All data are publicly available and sources are disclosed (see README file). All data series are included in the replication package.

title: Does Foreign Borrowing Lift Growth?
abstract: External borrowing by governments is widely viewed as an important instrument for financing development, yet its growth effects remain controversial. We exploit the bilateral structure of public sector lending relationships to construct plausibly exogenous foreign credit supply shocks, isolating changes in borrowing capacity arising from creditorspecific shifts in lending rather than borrower demand. Using data covering 134 developing economies over 1970-2023, we show that positive foreign credit supply shocks lead to persistent increases in public investment and external indebtedness. However, easier access to external public sector finance does not, on average, generate sustained improvements in output or productivity and is accompanied by real exchange rate appreciation, weaker external balances, and partial crowding-out of private investment. The macroeconomic benefits of external public sector borrowing depend critically on institutional quality. Countries with stronger institutions translate additional borrowing into more favorable productivity and output responses, while accumulating more public capital and relying less on domestic financing. Our findings suggest that greater access to external finance is not, by itself, sufficient to boost development. The effectiveness of public sector borrowing depends fundamentally on the institutional capacity to allocate and manage borrowed resources productively.

title: Risk-Sharing Tests and Covariate Shocks: Drought, Floods, and Pests in Uganda
abstract: Efficient risk sharing implies a simple factor structure for marginal utilities of expenditure (MUEs): Pareto weights divided by a common price. The standard approach infers MUEs from total expenditures, implicitly assuming homothetic preferences, unitary income elasticities, and identical price elasticities. Risk-sharing tests using total expenditures work for idiosyncratic shocks (budgets change, but not prices), but not “covariate” shocks (prices change). I describe all preferences that permit one to infer MUEs from expenditures and estimate nonhomothetic MUEs to test whether covariate shocks are shared efficiently in Uganda. This delivers sensible results; the standard approach suggests that droughts, floods, and pests are beneficial. (JEL D12, D81, O12, O13, Q12)

title: Assessing the effects of recent provisioning rules on consumer credit allocation in Colombia
abstract: In January 2023, Colombia introduced new banking rules. These rules required banks to set aside more money to cover risks from long-term consumer loans. This paper looks at how these changes affected banks and their lending practices.

title: Geopolitical risk and emerging market sovereign risk premia
abstract: This study examines the determinants of sovereign risk, focusing on the impact of geopolitical risk in emerging market economies (EMEs) sovereign risk metrics. Using local projection techniques, we evaluate the effects of geopolitical risk on credit default swaps (CDS) and EMBI indices in EMEs, including the recent war between Ukraine and Russia. Our findings highlight the significance of considering geopolitical risk when analyzing risk premiums for emerging markets. Notably, we find that the impact of geopolitical risk shocks on CDS is higher than the effect on EMBI spread dynamics. Furthermore, using recursive estimations, we show that the effect of geopolitical risk on sovereign CDS and EMBI spreads has been relatively stable. On the other hand, we find an important degree of heterogeneity across countries by analyzing evidence from individual countries. Some countries in our sample seem statistically unaffected by geopolitical risk, particularly when examining EMBI dynamics.

title: Jenseits des Gesamtwachstums: Russlands uneinheitliche Kriegswirtschaft
abstract: Seit der groß angelegten Invasion in die Ukraine zeigt die russische Wirtschaft je nach Sektor uneinheitliche Entwicklungen.Dieser Artikel untersucht anhand von Statistiken zur russischen Industrie und zu Unternehmensgewinnen diese Unterschiede.In den mit dem Militär verbundenen Sektoren sind sowohl die Produktion als auch die Gewinne stark gestiegen, während viele zivile Industriezweige mit Produktionsrückgängen, geringeren Gewinnen und höheren Kosten zu kämpfen haben.Selbst innerhalb einzelner Branchen zeigen detaillierte Daten auf Produktebene erhebliche Schwankungen.Die Ergebnisse deuten darauf hin, dass sich das Wachstum Russlands in Kriegszeiten zunehmend konzentriert, was es immer schwieriger macht, das Wachstum aufrechtzuerhalten.

title: Options for Tax System Reform in Asia and the Pacific
abstract: Asian and Pacific economies face mounting fiscal pressures from high and rising debt and interest rates and significant spending needs in light of successive shocks. In the coming years, these fiscal strains will likely be exacerbated by the fiscal implications of structural trends in demography, technology, geoeconomic fragmentation, and climate transitions. To address these mounting fiscal challenges, domestic revenue mobilization will be imperative. Based on a comparative analysis with global peers, this paper provides an integrated assessment of the opportunities for enhanced revenue mobilization across the region, drawing on newly compiled data and indicators for cross-country revenue, tax design and tax administration. It documents comparatively low tax-to-GDP ratios and sizable tax potential, alongside marked differences in policy design and administrative capacity across income groups. The paper identifies five areas for reform for Asian and Pacific countries: strengthening value-added taxation; rationalizing corporate income tax incentives; expanding recurrent property taxation; accelerating digitalization in tax administration; and building public trust in tax administration. The appropriate sequencing differs across countries, but durable domestic revenue mobilization requires policy and administration to be treated as an integrated system, embedded in medium-term revenue strategies, and adapted to structural transitions and institutional capacity.

title: On Digital Currency as Property for the Purposes of Inclusion in the Debtor’s Bankruptcy Estate in Insolvency Cases
abstract: This article notes the differences between digital currency and things and property rights, highlighting legislator’s and courts’ approaches to defining digital currency as property under Article 128 of the Civil Code of the Russian Federation. It notes a tendency of the courts to consider digital currency as other property not only for the purposes of protecting the public interests and the interests of non-participants of the digital currency circulation, particularly when it is included in a debtor’s bankruptcy estate under Article 131 of the Russian Insolvency Law, but also to protect the interests of the digital currency owner or participants of its circulation.

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: Do Actions Match Words? Reassessing the Taylor Rule in an Emerging-Market Context
abstract: Backward-looking Taylor rules, widely used to characterize central bank behavior, can misrepresent policy when central banks base decisions on forecasts. This mischaracterization affects the assessment of credibility, defined as alignment between a central bank’s words and actions. We examine this issue in the context of India’s adoption of flexible inflation targeting (FIT) in 2015. Text analysis shows that the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) communication became more inflation-focused and forward-looking after FIT adoption. Yet backward-looking Taylor rules show no robust increase in responsiveness to realized inflation, suggesting lack of credibility. This misalignment disappears when we analyze policy-relevant information through a forward-looking lens. Using the RBI’s real-time inflation and output forecasts, we find significant responsiveness to expected inflation post-FIT. Hybrid reaction functions show that post-FIT policy responds to both expected and realized inflation. The analogous evolution in communication and conduct points to the RBI’s credibility. More broadly, our results demonstrate that hybrid reaction functions may better characterize emerging-market central bank behavior than purely backward- or forward-looking specifications.

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

source: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Corporate dollar debt and balance sheet effects: identification using Trump tweets
abstract: This paper revisits foreign exchange spillover effects via the balance sheet channel, exploiting exogenous shocks triggered by the US president Trump’s 2018 tweets of threatening imminent sanctions on Turkish exports. These tweets were politically driven and produced a large and unanticipated exchange rate shock within the Turkish economy, consequently providing a quasi-natural experiment to investigate the balance sheet channel of dollar-denominated corporate debt. Using quarterly data for 2013–2023 for firms listed on Borsa Istanbul, our difference-in-difference estimations around the window of Trump tweets show that firms with high net FX debt experienced a major decline in investment rates following the depreciation, whereas the control group remained largely unaffected. The identified impact is approximately twice the size of estimates obtained through standard panel data methods. Overall, this study contributes to the literature by providing a clear and rigorous identification strategy for FX spillover effects through the balance sheet channel.

title: Income Inequality and Intergenerational Mobility in Russia: Trends, Sources, and Measurement
abstract: This chapter documents trends in income and inequality in Russia from the collapse of the Soviet Union through 2025, drawing on official statistics, the existing literature, and household survey microdata. It also reviews evidence on intergenerational mobility. While there is a consensus that inequality dramatically increased during the 1990s, its post-2000 trajectory is contested. Initial household survey studies usually found a decline, whereas official statistics reported a comparatively stable Gini coefficient. Our analysis of Russia's major household surveys, harmonized using common measurement conventions, aligns with the survey-based literature, indicating that the Gini coefficient generally fell from approximately 0.45–0.48 in the early 2000s to 0.29–0.38 in the early 2020s. We further find that most inequality arises within rather than between regions, urban and rural areas, and education and occupation groups. Household labor-market attachment, region, and household composition account for the largest shares of the explained variance in log income. The large literature on inequality is complemented by a small literature on intergenerational mobility. Here, the various studies on intergenerational dynamics in education, occupation, and income across post-Soviet cohorts conclude that, even against the background of dramatic structural changes, family background remains strongly associated with children’s outcomes.

title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
abstract: Abstract Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. By exploiting the introduction of bioequivalence in Chile, we find that stronger regulation reduced the number of drugs in the market by 18% and increased average paid prices by 13%. We estimate a model of drug entry, certification, and demand to study how drug quality, aversion to generics, and certification costs shape the equilibrium effects of quality regulation. We find that quality regulation increased demand for generic drugs by resolving asymmetric information and reducing aversion to unbranded generics, which induced the entry of high-quality drugs in place of low-quality drugs. Consumer welfare increased despite higher prices and a lower number of firms. We compare minimum quality standards with alternative designs of quality regulation, including quality disclosure.

title: Promoting Women to Managerial Roles in the Bangladeshi Garment Sector
abstract: Women remain disadvantaged in promotion to managerial positions. We conduct a field experiment with 24 large garment factories in Bangladesh to test for inefficient representation of women among line supervisors. We identify the marginal female and male candidates for supervisory positions and randomly assign them to manage production lines. We document four findings: (1) In contrast to widespread negative beliefs about women's ability as supervisors at baseline, female candidates selected by the factories had similar skills to males; (2) during the trial, females performed worse than males, which we show is related to negative bias against them; (3) after the trial, however, many female candidates were retained as supervisors and, conditional on that, performed similar to males; and (4) after the end of our intervention, factories permanently increased the share of women among newly appointed supervisors. A conceptual framework of experimentation over discrimination rationalizes all these facts and cautions against the standard logic to test for discrimination: when there is uncertainty about the performance of the discriminated group, equal—or even worse—performance of the marginal candidates of that group is no longer sufficient to rule out inefficient discrimination.

title: Why Veil? Religious Headscarves and the Economic Role of Women
abstract: Abstract We show that the emergence of new economic opportunities that draw women away from their traditional domestic roles has significantly influenced the adoption of religious veiling. We measure the prevalence of veiling among young women across Indonesia’s districts for more than two decades by hand-coding around a quarter million photographs attached to Indonesia’s public high school registers. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation generated by international demand for Indonesia’s products, interacted with the gender and sectoral composition of local industries. Districts exposed to stronger positive economic shocks—and thus greater economic opportunities for women—exhibit higher rates of veiling adoption. Our findings suggest that veiling facilitates young women’s participation in formal labour markets while safeguarding their personal and social image in society.

title: Technológiai szuverenitás és zöld ipar: a kínai iparpolitika új korszaka
abstract: A tanulmány a kínai gazdaság zöld átállását a Made in China 2025 (MIC2025) program mentén elsősorban iparpolitikai és technológia szempontból vizsgálja. Ennek részeként bemutatja, hogy miként lépett túl Kína a „világ gyára” szerepkörön, milyen hosszú távú célrendszer szerint szerveződik a MIC2025, és hogyan épül be a zöld technológiai fejlesztés – a félvezetőktől a megújuló energián át az intelligens gyártásig –, valamint a zöld innováció a stratégiai ágazatok fejlesztési logikájába. Az elemzés arra a következtetésre jut, hogy a program vállalati szintű innovációs hatásai empirikusan kimutathatók, ugyanakkor erősen egyenlőtlenek régiók és tulajdonosi formák szerint, míg a környezeti célok számszerű teljesülése egyelőre vegyes képet mutat.

title: Evidence Package: Institutional Cover-up of Attempted Murder, Hospital Document Concealment, and Organized Corruption System — Okrazhen Sad Burgas, Prokuratura, KZLD, SEM — Dimitar Prodromov (Pomorie, Bulgaria, 2018-2026)

title: Optimal Public Transportation Networks: Evidence from the World's Largest Bus Rapid Transit System in Jakarta
abstract: Designing public transport networks involves trade-offs between coverage, service frequency, and direct service. We use the expansion of the bus system in Jakarta, Indonesia, to study these trade-offs. We analyze how new direct connections, changes in bus travel time, and wait-time reductions affect bus ridership and aggregate flows and estimate a transit network demand model by matching the route launch events. Commuters in Jakarta are 2–3 times more sensitive to wait time than bus time and inattentive to long routes. We develop a flexible framework to characterize optimal networks. A less concentrated network would increase ridership and commuter welfare. (JEL L92, L98, O18, R41, R42, R48)

title: Shareholder conflicts, institutional quality, and tax avoidance
abstract: Abstract This study combines institutional theory with the logic of mixed gambles to examine how disproportionate voting rights of majority shareholders influence corporate tax behavior in the institutional context of China. We find support for our theoretical prediction that disproportionate voting rights create greater incentive for tax avoidance in China. Moreover, we leverage the heterogeneity in institutional strength across China to explicitly examine the role of institutions in shaping the relationship between disproportionate voting rights and tax avoidance. Our study extends agency research on minority shareholder expropriation by showing that when disproportionate voting rights co-exist with institutional voids, greater costs are imposed on minority shareholders and on society in the form of lower tax revenue for social investment. Practically, our findings can help inform the regulatory debates about the societal consequences of corporate structuring mechanisms (dual class shares and pyramid ownership) that enable disproportionate voting rights and give dominant shareholders outsized control over corporate resources. Our results also advance knowledge regarding the consequences of weaker institutional environments for minority shareholders and society more broadly.

title: A Global DSGE Model for Oil-Dependent Economies
abstract: This paper develops a global DSGE model linking oil-dependent economies to the systemic economies, and applies it to the GCC countries. The model features a range of nominal and real rigidities, extensive macrofinancial linkages, and diverse spillover transmission channels. Its modular structure also encompasses common features of oil-dependent economies, including a state-owned oil company, a capital intensive oil extraction technology, a sovereign wealth fund, an oil consumption subsidy, and membership of an international oil cartel. The calibrated model is used to simulate global risk and domestic reform scenarios the GCC economies, revealing how their distinct structural characteristics shape their responses to shocks.

title: Zombie firms in emerging Asia: domestic and cross border implications
abstract: Zombie firms in emerging Asia: domestic and cross border implications This paper analyses the macroeconomic implications of zombie firms in Asian emerging market economies (EMEs) in both the domestic and cross-border contexts. We use firm-bank linked data for 10 EMEs over 2005–21. To identify the cross-border spillover channels of Asian EME zombie firms for inflation and growth in advanced economies (AEs), we consider both the trade-weighted and cross-border lending-weighted exposures of the AEs to the Asian EME zombie firms. We provide the first evidence that zombie-induced disinflation transmits across borders through global value chain (GVC) linkages, by identifying zombie prevalence in GVC-connected economies. We also conduct a direct horse race between the trade and bank lending channels of international zombie transmission. In addition, we provide micro-level evidence on the asymmetric behaviour of domestic versus foreign banks in evergreening analysis in the domestic and cross-border contexts. Finally, we fill a gap in the zombie firm literature, which has mostly looked at AEs, by focusing on Asian EMEs central to GVCs. First, we find that the number of zombie firms in Asian EMEs has increased significantly over 2005-21, sustained by evergreening by weak banks. Second, zombie prevalence domestically depresses firm performance, crowds out healthy firms and lowers inflation and GDP growth.

source: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Workforce Aging and Firm Productivity: Evidence from Türkiye
abstract: Abstract Does workforce aging lower firm productivity? We study this question for a large emerging economy using matched employer–employee records from Türkiye linked to firm balance sheets over 2013–2023, roughly 1.75 million firm–year observations. Identifying the relationship from within-firm variation, we find that a higher share of older workers is associated with modestly lower productivity: a one-unit increase in the share of workers aged 50 and above lowers value added per worker by about 8.3 %. Much of the larger raw correlation reflects sorting of younger workforces into more productive firms, but a precise negative effect survives selection. The average conceals pronounced heterogeneity: the penalty is about 11 % in manufacturing and routine-intensive services, roughly half as large in construction and trade, and statistically absent in agriculture. Interacting the firm’s age composition with task scores confirms the mechanism: the penalty is attenuated where non-routine interpersonal content is high and amplified where routine and analytical content are high. What matters is less the age of a workforce than the work it performs. This is among the first firm-level evidence on aging and productivity for a large emerging economy.

title: The role of ecotourism in regional environmental transformation: evidence from Chinese cities
abstract: Purpose This study evaluates whether city-level ecotourism certification can function as an effective indirect environmental policy instrument by reducing industrial pollution. It further identifies the channels through which such effects arise, and derives targeted implications for regional policy design. Design/methodology/approach We use the introduction of China's Prototype-zone of National Ecotourism Attractions (PNEA) pilot program as a quasi-natural experiment and employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach on panel data from 296 Chinese cities covering the period from 2007 to 2019. Findings We find that PNEA certification significantly reduces industrial pollution, particularly in reducing wastewater and sulfur dioxide emissions. The mechanisms driving this effect are the promotion of green technological innovation and an amplifying effect of digitalization on green industrial development. Originality/value This study is among the most comprehensive ones to directly link ecotourism to industrial emissions reduction, highlighting the potential role of ecotourism as a tool for regional sustainable development. By documenting structural effects on pollution and identifying innovation and digitalization as key enabling factors, the study offers actionable guidance for integrating ecotourism certification into broader environmental policy frameworks.

title: Macroeconomic Effects of Forced Displacement in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: This paper estimates the macroeconomic effects of forced displacement on host economies in SubSaharan Africa, drawing on cross-country panel data and country case studies of Burkina Faso, South Sudan, and Uganda to provide granular evidence on the consequences of spatial concentrations of forcibly displaced persons within countries. Estimates from a difference-in-differences local projections (LP-DiD) framework do not suggest that large refugee inflows significantly affect host-country GDP, inflation, or the current account balance over a five-year horizon. The effects on the primary fiscal balance also appear to be muted, yet this masks offsetting fiscal dynamics: government expenditures rise and fiscal revenues increase (mainly through taxes). These results are robust to restricting the control group to Sub-Saharan African economies. Under a broader treatment definition that captures the total displaced population (refugees and internally displaced persons), the GDP response turns significantly negative and intensifies with displacement severity, though this estimate is best interpreted as an upper bound because it cannot be fully separated from the effects of conflict itself that generates displacement. The cross-country findings are consistent with the case studies, which indicate generally muted effects on aggregate food inflation and wages. Beneath this muted aggregate response, however, a consistent pattern emerges across cases: prices of imported and processed staples rise, while those of locally produced cereals stay flat or fall. The case studies also yield mixed evidence regarding the impacts of displacement inflows on consumption and labor force participation, with such inflows reducing host employment in Burkina Faso but raising it in Uganda.

source: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
title: Türkiye’de Tarımsal Destekler ve Üretim İlişkisi
abstract: Küresel iklim değişikliği, jeopolitik belirsizlikler ve tarımsal girdi maliyetlerindeki artış, gıda arz güvenliğini ve tarımsal üretimin sürdürülebilirliğini ciddi biçimde tehdit etmektedir. Tarımsal destek politikaları hem üretim istikrarının sağlanması hem de kırsal gelirlerin korunması açısından kritik bir politika aracı olarak öne çıkmaktadır. Bu çalışma, Türkiye’de uygulanan tarımsal desteklerin bitkisel ve hayvansal üretim üzerindeki etkilerini ampirik olarak incelemeyi amaçlamaktadır. Analizde, Tarım ve Orman Bakanlığı Çiftçi Kayıt Sistemi’ne (ÇKS) kayıtlı işletmelere ait 2019–2023 dönemini kapsayan il ve ilçe düzeyinde panel veriler kullanılmıştır. Bitkisel üretimde mazot ve gübre desteği ile fark ödemeleri; hayvancılıkta ise buzağı ve çiğ süt destekleri temel politika değişkenleri olarak ele alınmıştır. Üretim ve verimlilik üzerindeki etkiler, ürün, bölge ve yıl sabit etkilerini içeren çoklu regresyon modelleri aracılığıyla tahmin edilmiştir. Modellerde ayrıca iklim koşulları ve yapısal özellikler kontrol edilmiştir. Elde edilen bulgular, bitkisel üretimde mazot ve gübre desteği ile fark ödemelerinin üretim miktarı ve verimlilik üzerinde istatistiksel olarak anlamlı ve pozitif etkilere sahip olduğunu göstermektedir. Bununla birlikte, desteklerin üretim hacmi üzerindeki etkisinin verimlilik artışına kıyasla daha güçlü olduğu tespit edilmiştir. Hayvancılık desteklerinde ise buzağı ve çiğ süt desteklerinin hayvan varlığını artırıcı yönde etkili olduğu, ancak verimlilik üzerindeki etkilerin daha sınırlı kaldığı görülmektedir. Ayrıca çalışma, tarımsal desteklerin üretim kapasitesini artırmada etkili olduğunu ortaya koymakla birlikte, uzun vadede verimlilik odaklı, hedefli ve yapısal dönüşümü destekleyen politika tasarımlarının önemine işaret etmektedir.

title: Productivity trends of Russian firms in 2018—2024
abstract: This paper examines total factor productivity (TFP) dynamics among Russian enterprises from 2018 to 2024, using translogarithmic production function estimates for 290 industries. To address endogeneity and functional dependence issues, we employ the Ackerberg—Caves—Frazer methodology with a control function approach. Our findings reveal distinct sectoral patterns. In mining, both simple average and value-added-weighted TFP rose during 2020—2021, then declined in 2022. Manufacturing exhibited steady TFP growth from 2018 to 2022, with a sharp acceleration in 2023, followed by divergent trajectories: value-addedweighted TFP continued to increase, while simple average TFP fell in 2024. In trade, simple average TFP dropped markedly in 2021—2022 and had not recovered to baseline levels by 2024. The services sector, hardest hit by the COVID-19 pandemic, displayed a volatile growth path, with contractions in 2020 and 2022. Across all sectors, cumulative growth in value-added-weighted TFP consistently outpaced that of simple average TFP, pointing to significant within-sector firm heterogeneity and suggesting that larger enterprises are more resilient to shocks.

title: Brief Introductory Remarks, Outlook 26: The New England Economic Forum, Hosted by the New England Bankers Associations
abstract: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President & CEO Susan M. Collins delivered brief, opening remarks and introduced the keynote speaker, Michelle W. Bowman, Vice Chair for Supervision at the Federal Reserve Board, at "Outlook 26: The New England Economic Forum." The event, hosted by the six New England Bankers Associations, is a forum for bankers and business leaders that focuses on sharing economic perspectives and insights.

title: Nonlinear Dynamics in Menu Cost Economies? Evidence from U.S. Data
abstract: We show that standard menu cost models cannot simultaneously reproduce the dispersion in the size of micro-price changes and the extent to which the fraction of price changes increases with inflation in the U.S. time-series. Though the Golosov and Lucas (2007) model generates fluctuations in the fraction of price changes, it predicts too little dispersion in the size of price changes and therefore little monetary nonneutrality. In contrast, versions of the model that reproduce the dispersion in the size of price changes and generate stronger monetary nonneutrality predict a nearly constant fraction of price changes.

title: Labor market change, income polarization and urban housing inequality: a comparative study of Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the interaction between labor market reforms and housing policies in Italy, Spain and the UK. Design/methodology/approach By providing a comparative legal analysis of significant policy changes at the macro level and a descriptive overview of the evolution of their main economic determinants – wages and housing prices – at the micro level, the study highlights the socioeconomic impact of these reforms and their contribution to urban disparities. Findings The analysis suggests that the implementation of labor market reforms aimed at increasing flexibility and competitiveness coincided with heightened precarity, particularly for low-wage and nonstandard workers across all countries. Research limitations/implications The analysis does not address causality. Practical implications The paper suggests that stratified labor policy and work deregulation have an impact on urban inequality and wage distribution at sub-city level. Social implications The study argues that these reforms, coupled with macro-events such as the increase in global trades and the advent of ICT, might have exacerbated the socioeconomic inequalities at both national and local levels over the last decades by disfavoring less skilled workers, particularly in large cities. Originality/value The originality of the paper lies in its integrated analysis of labor-market reforms and housing policies as jointly producing urban disparities. Rather than treating wage stagnation, employment precarity and housing unaffordability as separate phenomena, the paper connects them through a comparative framework covering Italy, Spain and the UK. Its contribution is also empirical and spatial: it combines national regulatory trajectories with city-level evidence from Milan, London and Madrid, showing how macro-level reforms translate into uneven urban outcomes. This multi-scalar approach offers a distinctive perspective on the legal, economic and territorial roots of contemporary inequality.

title: Structural forecast analysis
abstract: Summary: This paper shows how the structural representation of a vector autoregressive model can support forecast analysis. We offer a unified framework that formalizes how the structural form of the model can help form a narrative for two key statistics in real-time vector autoregressive forecasting: the forecast errors at the outturn of the data, and the consequent revisions of the forecast. We conduct an exercise on the United Kingdom, focusing on the inflation surge that started in 2022. We show that revisions to the inflation forecast were driven not only by contractionary supply-side shocks, but also by a mix of expansionary demand-side shocks, with an important role played by revised past shocks. However, we find that the role of demand shocks was subsequently revised downwards as new data vintages become available.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Open Banking: A Critical Piece in the Future of Financial Services
abstract: Open banking enables consumers to securely share data from their bank accounts with third-party service providers. By using application programming interfaces, open banking facilitates innovations such as Pay-by-Bank payments, instant bill payments, and cash-flow-based lending. While regulatory efforts are underway at both federal and state levels, technological and operational barriers and a lack of standardization continue to challenge widespread use of open banking in the United States.

title: Firms and the Gender Wage Gap: A Comparison of Eleven Countries
abstract: We quantify the role of gender-specific firm wage premiums in explaining the private-sector gender gap in hourly wages using a harmonized research design across 11 matched employer-employee datasets—ten European countries and Washington state, USA. These premiums contribute to the gender wage gap through two channels: women’s concentration in lower-paying firms (sorting) and women receiving lower premiums than men within the same firm (pay-setting). We find that firm wage premiums account for 10 to 30 percent of the gender wage gap. While both mechanisms matter, sorting is the predominant driver of the firm contribution to the gender wage gap in most countries. We document three patterns that are broadly consistent across countries: (1) women’s sorting into lower-paying firms increases with age; (2) women are more concentrated in low-paying firms with a high share of part-time workers; and (3) women receive about 90 percent of the rents that men receive from firm surplus gains.

title: Beyond the Numbers: Professional Forecasters’ Narratives about Inflation and Stock Market Performance
abstract: Professional forecasters' heterogeneous narratives about how inflation affects stock markets in 2023 rationalize their high disagreement regarding quantitative expectations for 12-month-ahead inflation and stock returns in December 2022. Professional forecasters causally update their return expectations in heterogeneous directions in response to information about the inflation outlook, depending on the narrative they entertain. Moreover, the narratives also affect their asset allocation in a hypothetical portfolio-choice experiment. Providing common signals does not necessarily lead to convergence of beliefs if agents subscribe to different narratives.

title: Are European Firms Financially Constrained?
abstract: We examine if European firms face binding financial constraints that explain Europe’s persistent scale-up gap. Using corporate tax changes as exogenous shocks and a "debt test", we analyze 7 million predominantly private firms across 20 euro area countries (2000–2022). A higher corporate tax rate increases the value of interest deductibility and, absent frictions, induces firms to increase leverage. We find that firms generally increase leverage after tax hikes, indicating constraints are not broadly binding. However, young firms and those in innovation-intensive industries show weaker responses. Among innovative firms, constraints vary: young firms appear unconstrained, while small, mature ones face binding constraints. Our findings suggest that financing frictions in Europe are concentrated among specific firm types at particular development stages, indicating that they are important at the critical scale-up stage.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Introducing Trimmed Imports and Exports
abstract: Trade flows are volatile and notoriously difficult to predict. This paper introduces trimmed import and export growth rates for the United States to help improve trade forecasts. We calculate the growth rates as a trimmed mean that strips out subcomponents with less predictive power. By separating the signal from the noise, our trimmed growth rates provide a better perspective on where aggregate imports or exports are heading, particularly at horizons four to 12 months ahead. Consequently, out-of-sample forecasts based on our trimmed growth rates reduce forecast errors by up to 15 percent relative to forecasts from aggregate import or export growth. These trimmed forecasts are simple to compute, outperform both naive forecasts and models that rely on a richer information set, and are particularly useful during episodes with heightened volatility. We update the trimmed growth rates monthly and make them publicly available.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco
title: Can Fiscal, AI, or Monetary News Explain the Rise in r∗?
abstract: Following decades of secular decline, many estimates of r∗—the natural or steady-state short-term real interest rate—have risen roughly 1 percentage point since 2020 in the United States. The most prominent explanations attribute this reversal to heightened expectations of rising government debt and faster productivity growth from artificial intelligence (AI). However, a high-frequency event study finds that news about fiscal and AI developments does not explain this increase. Furthermore, contrary to earlier evidence that persistent shifts in longer-term yields occurred around monetary policy meetings, we find that monetary policy news does not account for the recent rise in r∗.

title: The Decline of Student Visas and Its Implications
abstract: In the last year and a half, the debate over immigration policy centered on undocumented workers in the U.S. Legal immigration, on the contrary, has not faced significant changes that would directly limit the number of new legal immigrants coming into the country. Despite this being true on the aggregate, a specific visa category does seem to show a significant decrease in numbers: the F-1 student visa, which is the primary visa used by full-time international students. As shown in Figure 1a, issuance of nonimmigrant visa has followed a similar aggregate trend in 2025 as in previous years.

title: Teaching Safety Skills for Emergency Situations to Autistic Individuals: A Rapid Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Emergency situations are unexpected events that pose a threat of serious and immediate risk to safety. Difficulties in social communication and restricted behaviour mean that some autistic individuals may be vulnerable to harm during these events. However, skills can be taught to minimise this risk and increase the likelihood that autistic people can respond safely to such situations. This rapid review identified empirical studies teaching emergency related safety skills to autistic children and adults. Studies were assessed for quality against the What Works Clearinghouse standards. Forty studies were identified, with 143 autistic individuals (mean age 9.3 years, range 3–25 years) across 10 scenarios. A wide range of teaching methodologies were used, e.g., Behaviour Skills Training. Interventions that taught skills in the actual environment (in-situ) were most effective. Overall, the findings indicate positive outcomes in acquisition, generalisation and maintenance of skills. However, over half of the studies did not meet minimum quality standards, gaps remain in the range of scenarios addressed, and there is a notable scarcity of studies focused on skills acquisition for older autistic adults. There are opportunities to utilise technology-mediated environments such as Virtual Reality to teach skills in relation to events that are difficult to simulate.

source: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
abstract: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output.

title: Market Power Rose, Why Didn't Profits?
abstract: Over the past six decades, the power of American firms to charge prices above their production costs — which economists call "market power" — has grown. In 1960, prices averaged about 10 percent above the cost of producing an additional unit of output. By 2020, that gap had widened to 25 percent. One might expect those widening margins to show up as a lasting rise in the share of gross domestic product (GDP) flowing to profits. They did not, as profits have averaged about 16 percent of GDP since 1960 and have fluctuated widely but without a lasting upward trend. The gap between the price and the cost of one additional unit is what economists call a markup, and a high markup does not by itself imply a high profit. A software firm's offering illustrates the distinction. Writing the code, building and maintaining the platform, and advertising the product require large up-front expenditures, while serving one more customer costs almost nothing, so nearly every dollar of every license is markup. Thus, that high markup is not pure profit, since the business must use it to recover the fixed costs associated with simply being in business. In our recently updated 2023 working paper "The Micro-Aggregated Profit Share," we measure markups and profits for thousands of U.S. firms between 1956 and 2024. We find that rising markups have not produced a lasting rise in profits, for a reason the software firm example makes intuitive: The fixed bills those markups must cover have grown alongside them. What looks like six decades of accumulating pricing power has been met by an offsetting force: the rising cost of simply being in business.

title: Joint Child Custody and Interstate Migration
abstract: Joint custody following divorce is widespread, yet the implementation of joint custody is costly when individuals live in different states, so it affects interstate mobility. Migration of divorced fathers has fallen significantly more than that of married fathers. We show the causal effect of joint custody using two strategies. First, we survey divorced parents to elicit beliefs about the likelihood of interstate moves. Second, we use the staggered adoption of joint custody laws across U.S. states, and show a reduction in actual migration of 11 percentage points for fathers. For mothers, there is no impact on mobility from the adoption of joint custody, though there is suggestive evidence of beneficial labor market outcomes.

title: Welcoming Remarks, 2026 Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference: Shaping the Future of Finance and Payments, Organized by the Federal Reserve Banks of Boston, Atlanta, and Richmond
abstract: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President & CEO Susan M. Collins delivered welcoming remarks at the “2026 Technology-Enabled Disruption Conference: Shaping the Future of Finance and Payments.” She discussed how rapid technological advancements are shaping economic activity in meaningful ways and influencing economic outcomes, citing broad advances in artificial intelligence, digital platforms, and payments technologies. Collins also introduced the conference keynote speaker, Christopher J. Waller, a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The event, co-hosted by the Federal Reserve Banks of Atlanta, Boston, and Richmond, is part of a conference series that seeks to better understand emerging and ongoing technological innovations and their economic implications. This includes exploring how technology-enabled disruption impacts businesses, workers, and consumers, as well as its broader effects on the economy and economic opportunity.

title: How Do Import Tariffs Affect Aggregate Prices? Theory and Evidence from Canada
abstract: By how much do import tariffs raise aggregate prices? We develop a simple decomposition that separates the aggregate price effect of a tariff into three channels—cost pass-through, markup adjustments, and consumer substitution across varieties—and calibrate an oligopolistic competition model with endogenous markups to firm-level market shares for Canadian domestic producers, U.S. exporters, and rest-of-world suppliers. A 25% counter-tariff on U.S. imports raises Canada's aggregate price index by 0.66—well below the 1.25% that direct cost pass-through alone would predict. The dominant offsetting force is consumer substitution toward non-U.S. varieties, which reduces the price effect by 0.47 percentage points; markup adjustments, holding fixed pre-tariff market shares, contribute a further 0.26 percentage point decrease. The gap between cost pass-through and the true price effect widens sharply with the tariff rate: at a 50% tariff, cost pass-through alone predicts more than twice the true price effect.

title: Cross-Policy Risk Pricing
abstract: We show that interactions across government policies affect firms’ cost of equity capital. Exploiting the 2018–2019 U.S. tariff shocks and concurrent federal procurement spending, we find that firms facing higher tariff exposure earn higher subsequent risk premia, but this effect is substantially attenuated for firms receiving greater procurement. A one-standard-deviation increase in procurement attenuates about two-thirds of the tariff-related risk premium. Procurement is relatively more favorable for politically connected and economically vulnerable firms. Larger procurement inflows also attenuate tariff-induced declines in subsequent earnings. Together, these findings reveal a form of fiscal insurance in which government procurement partially offsets the financing and real consequences of tariff exposure.

title: From Pink Slips to Polling Stations: The Electoral Consequences of Mass-Layoff Announcements
abstract: We study how mass-layoff announcements affect electoral outcomes using a newly assembled dataset of US establishment-level administrative notices from the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act. A matched event study compares same-state counties with and without sizable WARN-announced layoffs. Controlling for local labor-market conditions, layoff announcements increase the Democratic-Republican vote margin by reducing Republican votes and increasing Democratic votes without clearly altering election winners or incumbent support. Effects appear across political offices, are not driven by manufacturing decline, and are geographically localized. The responses operate through turnout composition rather than vote switching and result in no policy-induced changes in transfer payments.

title: Making It a Priority: How State Workforce Goals and Higher Education Align
abstract: In order to ensure that a state's workforce development infrastructure is prepared to support their workforce needs, states seek to understand and publicize the jobs that will be in future demand. Occupational projections provide a glimpse into aggregate, long-term trends, but states seek more targeted information to align their supply of workers to meet any imminent shifts in demand. Since there is no national standard for how states determine these high-demand jobs, the criteria they choose provide insight into a state's economic and policy goals. Our analysis of the Fifth District shows that states often focus on jobs that are expected to experience occupational growth, earn higher mobility wages, and/or meet certain educational requirements. With the implementation of Workforce Pell and the recent reemergence of gainful employment regulations, there is increased pressure on higher education institutions — and community colleges in particular — to ensure that programs align with workforce needs. By providing information on occupations in the state that are in high demand or have strong growth potential, state leaders can shape individual decisions on skill development, education, and career pathways. These designations can also be used to help align education, workforce, and economic development policies around common goals.

title: Opening Remarks
abstract: Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President and CEO Anna Paulson opened the Bank's 10th Annual Fintech Conference with welcome remarks, sharing her thoughts on the economic outlook and monetary policy ahead of two days of discussion among bankers, fintech leaders, regulators, academics, consumer advocates, and innovators. "Over the past 10 years, this gathering has grown into one of the field's most valuable forums,” Paulson said. “The conference has consistently produced insights that shape how we think about fintech and the broader financial system."

source: Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City
title: Fixed Costs in the U.S. Banking System
abstract: Fixed costs account for an increasing share of operating expenses in the U.S. banking system. From 1995 to 2026, estimated fixed costs rose from 37 percent to 62 percent as a share of total noninterest expense. Over the same period, estimated marginal and average operating costs declined, loan spreads and net interest margins fell, and estimated loan markups increased by 21 percentage points. These trends are pervasive across banks but are most pronounced among large banks. We develop a model of bank industry dynamics with endogenous fixed costs to rationalize these long-run trends and examine pro-competitive effects. While competition increases credit supply, it decreases lending efficiency and increases bank risk-taking.
